title: NS-VLA: Towards Neuro-Symbolic Vision-Language-Action Models
claim: A symbolic planner decomposes a long instruction into ordered sub-steps, and a neural policy executes each step in a closed loop.
layout: Stacked rows top-to-bottom, left legend column, closed feedback loop with t+1 arrow
description: The figure shows the NS-VLA pipeline in stacked horizontal bands. At the top, a purple user box holds the instruction "put the black bowl in the bottom drawer of the cabinet and close it". The text is underlined in blue, green and orange for the three sub-steps, and a scene photo sits beside it. An Encoder arrow leads to a symbolic row of primitive steps: pick bowl (checked), place in drawer (highlighted green, with a pointer pin), and close it (dashed orange). A green arrow leads down to the Solver row. There, an environment image feeds a chip-icon VLA policy with inputs I_t and S_t, and the policy outputs an action chunk A_t to a gripper. A t+1 loop returns to the environment. The bottom row shows simulation frames labelled pick, place and close, each with a check mark. A left column labels symbolic, neural and milestone, with a dashed feedback arrow. Colors map blue, green and orange to the stages.
caption: NS-VLA plans, then acts step by step.
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models ground natural-language instructions in visual observations to generate actions for robotic manipulation. On long-horizon tasks, existing VLA models face structure-blind backbones, backbone-bound generalization, and flat single-objective optimization. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Neuro-Symbolic Vision-Language-Action (NS-VLA) framework. It introduces a Neuro-Symbolic Encoder that parses the instruction into a primitive plan tracked by a gated monotone stage pointer, a Neuro-Symbolic Solver that conditions a chunked VLA policy on the active sub-instruction, and Hierarchical Joint Policy Optimization, which fits the pointer on demonstration segments and refines the action policy with success-filtered online learning. Even when trained on few demonstrations, NS-VLA clearly leads on LIBERO and the held-out LIBERO-Plus (76.5% and 51.8% against 71.2% and 45.4% for its backbone), exceeds the strongest baseline by 12.7 points on long-horizon tasks, and raises real-robot success from 40.0% to 60.0%. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Zuzuzzy/NS-VLA.
